Hypothesis: Phase-resolved optical spectroscopy plus multiband time-series photometry of millisecond-pulsar binaries in NGC 6752 can deliver likelihood-dominated (not prior-dominated) constraints on orbital inclination i, companion filling factor f_RL, companion mass M2 (including discrimination between HeWD and massive CO/ONe WD companions), and neutron-star mass MNS, by jointly fitting (1) a radial-velocity (RV) curve and phase-dependent line profiles that constrain K2, vrot sin i, Teff(phase), and log g, and (2) multiband light curves whose ellipsoidal harmonics and Doppler boosting encode i and f_RL once distance/reddening and atmosphere physics are controlled. The mechanism for breaking the dominant optical degeneracy (i–f_RL–Teff/albedo–distance/reddening–asymmetric heating) is explicit: (a) the RV mass function + rotational broadening ties i and f_RL through vrot sin i ≈ (2πR2/Pb) sin i (with R2 set by Roche geometry and f_RL), thereby converting the usual photometric i–f_RL degeneracy into a constrained geometric problem; (b) WD/MS atmosphere models (composition-dependent) connect the observed SED and line blanketing to Teff and log g, which—combined with cluster distance and reddening hyperparameters—yields a radius R2 estimate and thus a second, independent constraint on f_RL; (c) physically motivated irradiation with controlled asymmetry (wind/shock offset + heat redistribution) explains phase shifts and unequal maxima without resorting to an unconstrained temperature map that would reabsorb inclination information. The neutron-star EoS/TOV coupling is not used to claim direct optical sensitivity to (M,R); instead, EoS inference is restricted to what is supported by likelihood pathways: MNS from timing mass function + optical K2 (+ i from the joint model) and, where available, WD mass from (log g, R2) combined with finite-temperature WD mass–radius relations. A TOV/EoS prior is applied only at the final stage as a consistency filter (causality/max-mass) on the resulting MNS posteriors, unless simulations demonstrate measurable sensitivity to relativistic photometric terms at the achieved precision.
Plan:
Step 0 — Target and data audit (NGC 6752-specific).
0.1 Target list: start with PSR J1911−5958A (COM J1911−5958A) as the anchor system (known optical counterpart; inclination already constrained >70° in prior work). Add any additional MSP binaries with published timing solutions and candidate counterparts from HST/VLT deep imaging catalogs; include IMBP candidates (optically brighter, potentially massive WDs) if present.
0.2 Membership and contamination screening: require (i) counterpart proper motion consistent with NGC 6752 (Gaia/HST PM where available), (ii) CMD position consistent with WD/MS companion locus at cluster distance, (iii) systemic velocity consistency with cluster radial velocity within uncertainties. Flag ambiguous cases and model non-membership as a mixture component in the likelihood.

Step 1 — Observing program with quantified requirements (spectroscopy + photometry).
1.1 Spectroscopy requirements (K2, log g, vrot sin i):
- Telescope/instrument class: 8–10 m (e.g., VLT/FORS2 or X-shooter; Gemini/GMOS; Magellan/IMACS for imaging + MagE for spectroscopy), chosen based on counterpart magnitude and crowding.
- Spectral resolving power: baseline R ≈ 6000–10000 (Δv ≈ 30–50 km/s) to recover K2 at ≤5–10 km/s and measure vrot sin i ≳ 30 km/s (or place informative upper limits). For bright IMBP WD counterparts (if V≲22–23), target R ≈ 10000; for faint (V≈23–25), accept R≈6000 with more epochs.
- Phase sampling: ≥12 spectra uniformly spaced in orbital phase for Pb≈8.8 h (PSR J1911−5958A-like), with exposure times capped to limit phase smearing to <0.03 cycles per exposure (Δt < 0.03 Pb ≈ 950 s for Pb=8.8 h). Prefer 18–24 epochs to diagnose asymmetric heating (line strength/Teff variation).
- Per-epoch SNR: design for SNR≈10–15 per resolution element in the continuum (or in key lines) to enable cross-correlation RVs and atmosphere fitting; if only SNR≈5–8 is feasible, prioritize K2 via template cross-correlation and treat log g constraints as weaker with explicit inflation.
- Wavelength coverage: include Balmer lines for DA WDs (Hβ–Hδ region) and He lines for DB/HeWD candidates; include blue-optical (≈380–520 nm) where line diagnostics are strongest, plus red-optical for SED anchoring if possible.

1.2 Photometry requirements (ellipsoidal + color curves under crowding):
- Instrumentation: HST (WFC3/UVIS) preferred for crowding-limited fields; if ground-based, use AO-assisted imagers when possible; otherwise difference-image analysis (DIA) on seeing-limited data.
- Bands: at minimum 3 bands spanning blue-to-red (e.g., U/B, V, I) to constrain Teff and reddening degeneracy; ideally 5 bands (U,B,V,R,I) but not required if spectroscopy provides Teff/log g.
- Cadence: ≥100 phase points per band over ≥2 orbits to average stochastic variability and mitigate systematics. For Pb≈8.8 h, cadence ≈2–5 min (exposure+overhead) is sufficient.
- Photometric precision target: ≤0.01–0.02 mag per point for detecting ellipsoidal harmonics and Doppler boosting at the few percent level; if only 0.03–0.05 mag is achievable, rely more heavily on RV + vrot sin i constraints and report reduced identifiability.
- Cross-epoch calibration: if simultaneous multiband is not feasible, interleave bands with strict barycentric time-stamping and apply nightly zeropoint tying using cluster standards; propagate calibration uncertainty explicitly.

1.3 Crowding/blending mitigation plan:
- Use PSF-fitting photometry (DAOPHOT/DOLPHOT or equivalent) and forced photometry at the timing position.
- Inject-and-recover artificial stars near each target to quantify blending bias and photometric error under local crowding.
- Include a “third-light” (blend flux) parameter per band in the forward model with priors anchored by high-resolution imaging; this prevents inclination bias from unmodeled contamination.

Step 2 — Forward model architecture (explicitly constrained; controlled complexity).
2.1 Orbital and Roche geometry:
- Use exact binary relations for the mass function and Keplerian geometry.
- Companion surface: Roche equipotential with filling factor f_RL ∈ (0.7, 1.0] (or broader if justified by CMD radius constraints).
- Surface brightness includes gravity darkening and limb darkening using atmosphere-specific coefficients (not generic). For convective envelopes (MS-like), allow β≈0.08; for radiative, β≈0.25; for WD companions, treat as radiative.

2.2 Spectroscopic component (likelihood-driving constraints):
- RV model: K2, γ (systemic), phase zero-point tied to radio timing ephemeris with allowed small offset (Gaussian prior from timing uncertainty).
- Rotational broadening: compute vrot sin i from R2 and synchronous rotation assumption; include a parameter for asynchronism (Ω/Ωsync) with tight prior centered on 1 (width set by tidal timescale expectations), to avoid bias if not perfectly locked.
- Atmosphere inference: fit Teff and log g using grids:
  * HeWD grids (He atmosphere; appropriate line diagnostics), DA/DB WD grids, and (if non-degenerate companion is plausible) low-mass MS atmosphere grids.
  * Include composition class as a discrete model with evidences compared (Bayes factors) rather than forcing a single choice.
- Emulator policy: use an interpolator/emulator only as a speed layer; enforce validation by (i) k-fold cross-validation on the grid, (ii) maximum interpolation error budget (e.g., ΔTeff < 1–2%, Δlog g < 0.05–0.1 dex where SNR permits), (iii) explicit nuisance inflation if the target sits near grid edges.

2.3 Photometric component:
- Ellipsoidal modulation computed from Roche geometry + atmosphere limb/gravity darkening; fit per band simultaneously.
- Doppler boosting included with bandpass-dependent beaming factor derived from the fitted SED slope (not assumed constant).
- Extinction: hierarchical E(B−V) model with (i) cluster mean prior, (ii) per-target differential reddening offset, and (iii) residual scatter term constrained by nearby stars.
- Distance: hierarchical distance modulus prior from cluster measurements; allow small depth dispersion for NGC 6752 and propagate to R2.
- Third light: per-band additive flux with informative priors from image decomposition.

2.4 Irradiation and asymmetry model (physically motivated; limited degrees of freedom):
- Base heating: incident flux Finc(θ,φ) ∝ Lirr / (4πa^2) × cosψ, truncated at zero for the nightside.
- Reprocessing efficiency: parameter ε (combining albedo and thermalization) with physically bounded prior ε∈[0,1].
- Heat redistribution: single parameter η controlling day-to-night diffusion (e.g., η=0 no redistribution; η→1 strong smoothing). Implement via a low-order solution of a diffusion/relaxation operator rather than free spherical harmonics, to prevent the map from absorbing inclination.
- Asymmetry from intrabinary shock / wind anisotropy: include one hotspot-offset term: shift the sub-pulsar heating pattern by an angle Δφshock (prior centered near 0 with width informed by typical black-widow/redback offsets), plus an amplitude modifier Ashock. This captures phase shifts and unequal maxima with only 2 extra parameters.
- Optional complexity control: only introduce higher-order asymmetry if posterior predictive checks demand it (Bayesian model comparison).

Step 3 — Identifiability, requirements, and simulation-based error budget (mandatory directive).
3.1 Synthetic data generation (NGC 6752-quality):
- Build end-to-end mock datasets with crowding noise, third-light contamination, differential reddening residuals, and realistic cadence.
- Simulate multiple regimes: (A) HeWD-like companion (Teff~10–20 kK), (B) massive WD companion (CO/ONe; higher log g), (C) MS-like companion (if applicable), across inclinations i=50–85°, filling factors f_RL=0.8–1.0, and plausible ε,η,Δφshock.
- Include instrument-specific throughput and resolution to match the planned setups.

3.2 Parameter identifiability matrix (what the likelihood constrains):
- Run inference on mocks under incremental model stacks:
  S0: photometry-only, phenomenological heating;
  S1: + multiband + extinction/distance hierarchical;
  S2: + RV curve (K2);
  S3: + vrot sin i constraint from line profiles;
  S4: + atmosphere grid constraints on Teff/log g;
  S5: + physically bounded irradiation with η and Δφshock;
  (Optional) S6: + relativistic beaming refinement.
- For each stack, report expected posterior widths (e.g., σi, σMNS, σM2, σf_RL) and mutual information / Bayes factors relative to simpler stacks.
- Define success criteria before observing: e.g., σi ≤ 2–3° and σMNS ≤ 0.1–0.2 Msun for the anchor system under achievable SNR; relaxed goals for fainter targets.

3.3 K2/log g recoverability validation:
- Inject known K2 and vrot sin i into synthetic spectra and test recovery under R and SNR conditions; quantify bias vs. phase smearing and template mismatch.
- For log g, quantify the minimum SNR/R required to distinguish HeWD-like (log g~6–7) from massive WD (log g~8–9) at >3σ, or state explicitly when log g becomes non-identifiable and classification must rely on CMD radius + WD cooling tracks.

3.4 Decision on TOV/EoS coupling:
- Baseline: do not use TOV priors to tighten i or heating parameters.
- Only if simulations show detectable optical sensitivity to relativistic photometric terms at achieved precision (e.g., Doppler boosting detected at >5σ and consistent across bands), consider adding compactness-dependent terms; otherwise restrict EoS inference to mapping the measured MNS distribution to EoS hyperposteriors with causality/max-mass constraints.

Step 4 — Inference and deliverables.
4.1 Bayesian inference engine: HMC/NUTS for continuous parameters; reversible-jump or marginalization for discrete atmosphere class (DA/DB/HeWD/MS). Parameterization uses cos i, log f_RL, and bounded transforms for ε,η.
4.2 Outputs per system:
- i, K2, q, MNS, M2 with full covariance;
- Companion classification probability (HeWD vs massive WD vs other);
- Evidence for irradiation asymmetry (Δφshock) and redistribution (η);
- Blend flux posteriors and quality-of-fit diagnostics.
4.3 Population/cluster-level analysis:
- Hierarchical modeling of distance modulus, reddening field residuals, and a contamination fraction.
- Correlate inferred companion type and system parameters with projected cluster-centric radius to test exchange-encounter predictions.

Step 5 — External benchmarking.
5.1 Validate the pipeline on field eclipsing/high-inclination systems where i is independently known (e.g., eclipsing AMXP-like geometry constraints) by degrading data to NGC 6752 SNR/cadence and confirming unbiased recovery of i and masses.
5.2 Reproduce published results for PSR J1911−5958A-like systems as a sanity check, then demonstrate posterior tightening attributable specifically to adding vrot sin i + atmosphere + controlled-asymmetry irradiation.
Feasibility:
Empirical basis and pathway to constraints: Prior optical work on an NGC 6752 MSP companion already demonstrates inclination constraints >70° from RV+photometry; optical detection of IMBP companions shows massive WDs are observable with large telescopes. The revised plan makes the primary information channels explicitly likelihood-driven: K2 provides q through the mass function; vrot sin i + Roche geometry constrains R2 sin i and thus i and f_RL; atmosphere-based Teff/log g + cluster distance/reddening yields R2 and an independent handle on f_RL and WD type; multiband ellipsoidal harmonics and Doppler boosting add inclination leverage once third light and reddening are controlled.

Addressing reviewer doubts about EoS coupling: The proposal no longer claims that neutron-star compactness measurably imprints on the companion’s optical light curve in typical MSP+WD systems. TOV/EoS enters only after obtaining MNS posteriors from timing + optical constraints, as a physically consistent mapping to EoS families (causality/max-mass), unless simulations demonstrate an actual measurable optical pathway at the achieved precision.

Quantified requirements and crowding realism: The observing plan specifies telescope class, resolving power, SNR targets, phase sampling, and phase-smearing limits appropriate to Pb~hours binaries, and it incorporates cluster-specific systematics (crowding/blending, differential reddening, depth) as explicit nuisance parameters with priors informed by artificial-star tests and high-resolution imaging. This prevents under-modeled blending from masquerading as inclination or heating asymmetry.

Controlled irradiation complexity: Instead of an unconstrained spherical-harmonic temperature map, the heating model uses a bounded efficiency ε, a single redistribution parameter η, and a minimal physically motivated asymmetry term (Δφshock, Ashock). Complexity is only increased if demanded by posterior predictive checks, limiting the risk that flexible maps absorb inclination information.

Mandatory identifiability analysis: The plan includes an end-to-end simulation program that will report posterior shrinkage and identifiability under incremental model stacks, demonstrating which parameters are actually constrained for NGC 6752-quality data and defining success/failure criteria before full execution.
Critique: The proposal is methodologically mature and unusually explicit about degeneracy breaking, with a credible pathway to being likelihood-dominated: (i) K2 + timing mass function constrains q, (ii) vrot sin i provides a geometric tie between i and f_RL under (near-)synchronous rotation, and (iii) atmosphere-model Teff/log g + cluster distance/reddening yields an independent R2 constraint. The inclusion of third-light parameters and artificial-star tests is a strong, necessary crowding control for NGC 6752. However, several key risks remain under-quantified: (1) the feasibility of measuring vrot sin i at the required precision for V~23–25 companions with R~6000–10000 and SNR~10–15 is marginal, and line-profile systematics from irradiation-driven Teff gradients can bias rotational broadening unless explicitly forward-modeled; (2) the assumption of synchronous rotation and Roche geometry is central—small asynchronism, underfilling, or non-standard WD line broadening (Stark pressure, Zeeman/magnetic fields) can mimic/obscure rotation and log g, weakening the claimed inclination leverage; (3) discrimination between HeWD (log g~6–7) and massive CO/ONe WD (log g~8–9) is plausible in principle but, for heated/crowded/faint targets, Balmer/He line fitting may become prior-dominated by atmosphere-grid systematics and cluster distance/extinction hyperpriors; (4) Doppler boosting and ellipsoidal harmonics at few-percent amplitude are vulnerable to blending, differential reddening, and bandpass-dependent calibration, and the plan would benefit from a more explicit end-to-end requirement flowdown (precision on K2, vrot sin i, log g -> σi -> σMNS) tied to actual exposure-time calculations for NGC 6752 targets. The EoS/TOV boundary is handled responsibly (used only as a consistency filter), which improves logical integrity and avoids overclaiming optical compactness sensitivity.

Hypothesis:
A nanohertz stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) induces a tensor–transverse (TT) sky-correlated spin-1 astrometric proper-motion field whose two-point statistics are optimally extracted only if (i) Gaia’s dominant scan-synchronous/global systematics are modeled as explicit low-dimensional nuisance modes and analytically marginalized, and (ii) the TT signal is treated as a forward response from an underlying TT metric perturbation to catalog-level observables with full survey window/mask mode-coupling accounted for. We hypothesize that a scan-aware, generative ‘marginalized TT-needlet’ estimator—built from (a) a localized spin-1 spherical needlet representation for multi-scale, spatially inhomogeneous weighting; (b) a forward TT response operator that predicts the coupled E/B-mode covariance of proper motions under the Gaia window; and (c) an exact Gaussian likelihood (or equivalently an optimal quadratic estimator) in coefficient space with analytic marginalization over calibration/attitude nuisance modes—will deliver (1) higher calibrated detection SNR and (2) less biased, tighter constraints on characteristic strain h_c(f_ref) and band-integrated Ω_GW compared to (A) free quadrupolar VSH coefficient fits and (B) post-hoc binned astrometric Hellings–Downs (HD) curves.

Mechanism (why this resolves the review risks):
1) Replacing ad-hoc catalog-level cross-covariance ‘whitening’ with a principled generative model prevents absorbing true SGWB correlations into an empirically estimated N. The nuisance-mode marginalization treats scan/attitude/calibration systematics as a structured low-rank component (not an unconstrained covariance field), separating them from the TT correlation signature by exploiting their distinct angular/mode content and priors informed by Gaia scanning geometry.
2) Instead of a hard TT projector that can induce signal loss under masking/noise anisotropy, we implement TT-ness as a forward-model constraint: the SGWB predicts a specific coupled covariance between spin-1 E/B components after applying the survey window (pseudo-C_ℓ-like mode coupling). This yields a controlled transfer function that quantifies leakage and preserves optimality.
3) The detection statistic is derived from the exact Gaussian likelihood with correct normalization (log-determinants) and a rigorously derived quadratic form (matched filter / optimal quadratic estimator) whose null distribution is calibrated via end-to-end simulations, enabling reliable false-alarm control.
4) For nuclear/EOS physics: Gaia’s ultra-low-frequency, band-integrated response provides limited spectral discrimination, so EOS dependence cannot generally be claimed as strongly “informative” on its own. We therefore re-scope the EOS component to (i) a physically constrained sub-dominant fraction of Ω_GW with explicit identifiability tests (Fisher/Bayes factors) and (ii) consistency/upper-bound statements on an NS contribution under EOS-feasible spectra, rather than asserting robust EOS measurement. This prevents prior-dominated decomposition from being over-interpreted while still leveraging physical constraints to rule out unphysical spectra masquerading as TT correlations.
Plan:
Step 0 — Data products, observables, and notation (explicit Gaia realism)
0.1 Observable: use Gaia quasar proper motions μ_i ≡ (μ_α*, μ_δ)_i with per-source 2×2 covariance C_i from the catalog; treat these as noisy estimates of the sky-projected time derivative of astrometric deflection integrated over Gaia’s mission window.
0.2 Mask/window: define a sky mask M(n̂) using Galactic latitude cuts, known problematic regions, and source-level quality cuts (RUWE/excess noise/duplicated_source/etc.). Represent M as a pixel-space weight and propagate it into harmonic/needlet space to compute mode-coupling matrices.
0.3 Frequency response: define Gaia’s effective temporal response W(f) from the mission time sampling and baseline (e.g., an effective low-frequency window with high-pass behavior at f ≲ 1/T and suppression at f ≫ cadence scale). All SGWB constraints are explicitly reported as W(f)-weighted band integrals.

Step 1 — Replace empirical N with a scan-/attitude-/calibration-mode generative noise model (mandatory directive)
1.1 Noise decomposition (catalog level): model the proper-motion data vector d (stacked over sources and components) as
    d = s_TT(θ_GW) + A a + ε,
where s_TT is the SGWB-induced signal, A a is a low-dimensional nuisance-mode contribution, and ε is residual (approximately) uncorrelated noise with block-diagonal covariance N0 = diag(C_i) plus optional inflation for quasar jitter.
1.2 Nuisance-mode design matrix A (explicit mode families): construct A from a union of physically motivated global/large-scale systematics modes that are known to dominate Gaia astrometry at low multipoles and/or scan-synchronous patterns:
  (i) VSH rigid rotation and glide (ℓ=1 toroidal/spheroidal),
  (ii) low-order VSH fields (ℓ=2–ℓ_max,sys) capturing large-scale calibration drifts (choose ℓ_max,sys by evidence/Fisher tests, e.g., 5–10),
  (iii) scan-synchronous modes parameterized by Gaia spin phase / precession geometry mapped onto the sky as templates (constructed from public scanning-law tools; at minimum, include basis functions correlated with along-scan (AL) parallax-factor-like patterns and large-scale AL calibration harmonics),
  (iv) optional chromaticity/color-dependent templates if color systematics are suspected (using BP/RP color as a regressor mapped to sky).
Each column of A is a 2N_src-length template predicting (μ_α*, μ_δ) contributions at each source location.
1.3 Prior on nuisance amplitudes: impose a Gaussian prior a ~ N(0, Σ_a) with Σ_a diagonal or block-diagonal by mode family. Hyperparameters (mode-family variances) are inferred or profiled, with weakly informative priors anchored to known Gaia systematics scales (ensuring the model is flexible enough to absorb calibration artifacts but not arbitrary to the point of eating TT correlations).
1.4 Analytic marginalization: integrate out nuisance parameters a to obtain an effective covariance
    C_tot(θ_GW) = S_TT(θ_GW) + N0 + A Σ_a A^T,
and a marginalized likelihood p(d | θ_GW, hyper) = N(0, C_tot) (after mean subtraction if needed). This implements “whitening” in a principled low-rank + diagonal form rather than requiring unavailable cross-source covariances.

Step 2 — TT forward response and survey window: from SGWB to catalog proper motions (addresses TT-projector critique)
2.1 Underlying TT field: parameterize the SGWB by Ω_GW(f) (or equivalently characteristic strain h_c(f)) with a reference amplitude and spectral index for SMBHB-like components, plus an optional NS component constrained by EOS-feasible families.
2.2 Signal covariance in harmonic space (full-sky theory): use the known GR prediction that an isotropic TT SGWB induces correlated astrometric deflections/proper motions with a specific E/B structure (spin-1 field with predicted C_ℓ^{EE}, C_ℓ^{BB}, and cross-terms as applicable for the astrometric observable). Express the theoretical full-sky covariance of harmonic coefficients as
    ⟨a_{ℓm}^X a_{ℓ'm'}^{X'}⟩ = δ_{ℓℓ'}δ_{mm'} C_ℓ^{XX'}(θ_GW),
with X, X' ∈ {E,B} for spin-1.
2.3 Window/mask mode coupling (pseudo-C_ℓ logic): propagate M(n̂) and inhomogeneous weights into an explicit coupling operator K such that the observed (masked) coefficients satisfy
    a_obs = K a_true + noise.
Compute K (or its action) numerically using spherical harmonic transforms or needlet-domain equivalents. This replaces “hard TT nulling” with a forward model that predicts how TT power leaks under the survey window.
2.4 TT ‘projection’ as a transfer-calibrated filter: define an operator F_TT that constructs the optimal linear combination of observed spin-1 components that maximizes TT-SGWB SNR given K and C_tot (i.e., a Wiener/matched filter in coefficient space). Quantify its transfer function T_ℓ (signal attenuation vs ℓ) and leakage into null channels under masking.

Step 3 — Needlet-domain architecture (localization retained, now survey- and likelihood-consistent)
3.1 Spin-1 needlet transform: transform the vector proper-motion field into spin-1 needlet coefficients β_{j,k} (band j, spatial index k). Use a specified needlet construction (e.g., compactly supported window b_j(ℓ) with overlap) and choose j-bands to emphasize low multipoles where the astrometric HD/TT signature is concentrated, while allowing localized downweighting of contaminated sky regions.
3.2 Data model in needlet space: write β = B d, where B is the linear needlet transform. Then
    Cov(β) = B C_tot B^T.
Exploit the structure C_tot = N0 + AΣ_aA^T + S_TT(θ) to compute matrix-vector products efficiently (diagonal + low-rank + structured signal).
3.3 No “full cross-source whitening” claim: implement inference using either (i) iterative solvers for C_tot^{-1}·v in needlet space or (ii) Woodbury identities for the low-rank nuisance term:
    (N0 + AΣ_aA^T)^{-1} = N0^{-1} − N0^{-1}A(Σ_a^{-1}+A^TN0^{-1}A)^{-1}A^TN0^{-1}.
This yields exact marginalization/weighting under the assumed generative model without needing unavailable Gaia pairwise covariances.

Step 4 — Exact likelihood and optimal detection statistic (addresses critique iv)
4.1 Gaussian log-likelihood: use
    ln L(θ_GW) = −1/2 [ d^T C_tot(θ_GW)^{-1} d + ln det C_tot(θ_GW) + n ln(2π) ].
Compute ln det via matrix determinant lemma for the nuisance low-rank part plus stochastic trace/log-det estimators if needed for the signal-dependent part.
4.2 Optimal quadratic estimator (optional implementation path): derive an optimal quadratic estimator for an amplitude parameter A_GW (or bandpowers) using
    \hat{A} ∝ d^T C^{-1} (∂C/∂A) C^{-1} d − Tr[C^{-1}(∂C/∂A)],
with Fisher normalization F = 1/2 Tr[C^{-1}(∂C/∂A)C^{-1}(∂C/∂A)]. This is the rigorous form corresponding to a properly normalized likelihood expansion.
4.3 Calibrated SNR and false-alarm: define SNR from either (i) likelihood ratio test statistic 2Δln L or (ii) \hat{A}/σ_A from Fisher theory, and calibrate its null distribution using end-to-end simulations that include the nuisance-mode prior and scanning-law templates.

Step 5 — Astrometric HD curve as a derived diagnostic, not the primary estimator (aligns with Asset 1)
5.1 From posterior/predicted C_ℓ^{EE/BB} to real-space correlation: compute the implied astrometric HD-like angular correlation function (proper-motion correlation vs separation) from the inferred TT signal model, including the survey window coupling. Use this as an interpretable diagnostic and cross-check against prior HD-curve approaches, but avoid using binned pair correlations as the primary likelihood object.
5.2 Systematics localization: exploit needlet localization to produce sky maps of residuals and jackknife stability metrics (drop-one-patch, rotate mask, scan-phase splits) to identify scan-synchronous contamination.

Step 6 — Astrophysical spectral model and identifiability (addresses critique v)
6.1 Baseline SGWB model: adopt Ω_GW(f) = Ω_BH(f; θ_BH) + η_NS Ω_NS(f; θ_NS, EOS), with η_NS ∈ [0,1] an explicit fractional amplitude parameter controlling the NS contribution.
6.2 EOS role re-scoped: EOS enters only through a constrained family of Ω_NS(f) shapes/amplitudes consistent with causality and maximum NS mass constraints. The primary deliverable is an upper limit or consistency bound on η_NS (or on an integrated NS contribution) rather than a claim of EOS measurement.
6.3 Fisher/identifiability study (mandatory): compute Fisher matrices (or simulation-based posteriors) for parameters {A_BH, α_BH, η_NS, …} under Gaia’s effective window W(f). Quantify degeneracies and demonstrate under what conditions (if any) Gaia can distinguish an NS-shaped component from an SMBHB-like power law. If identifiability is weak, freeze NS spectral shape and report only an upper limit on η_NS conditioned on EOS-feasible priors.

Step 7 — Validation program (explicitly tied to reviewer concerns)
7.1 End-to-end simulations with scanning-law systematics: generate synthetic catalogs with actual quasar sky positions, realistic per-source covariances, and injected nuisance modes A a drawn from Σ_a, plus optional additional scan-synchronous templates not included in A to test robustness.
7.2 SGWB injections: inject TT SGWB realizations consistent with the astrometric response, spanning amplitudes around current constraints (Asset 1) and spectral shapes motivated by PTA results (Asset 2) to test recovery and bias.
7.3 Transfer function and signal loss: measure the recovered amplitude vs injected amplitude to estimate the estimator transfer function under masking/mode coupling; require bias < predefined tolerance and quantify leakage into null combinations.
7.4 Benchmarking: compare against (i) quadrupolar VSH fits and (ii) pair-binned astrometric HD curves on identical simulations. Report SNR at fixed false-alarm, bias/variance on h_c and Ω_GW, and susceptibility to nuisance contamination.

Step 8 — Deliverables
8.1 A publicly documented pipeline implementing: (i) nuisance-mode construction A and Σ_a inference, (ii) TT forward covariance with window coupling, (iii) needlet-domain likelihood / quadratic estimator with Woodbury acceleration, (iv) simulation and calibration suite.
8.2 Science outputs: calibrated constraints on h_c(f_ref) and W(f)-weighted Ω_GW, plus derived astrometric HD-like correlation curves with uncertainty bands, and (if identifiable) a constrained bound on η_NS under EOS-feasible families.
Feasibility:
1) Consistency with actual Gaia products (addresses covariance realism): The revised approach no longer assumes unavailable catalog-level cross-source covariances. It uses only released per-source covariances (block-diagonal N0) plus an explicit low-rank generative model AΣ_aA^T for global/scan-synchronous correlations, which is exactly the regime where Gaia systematics are expected to dominate at low multipoles. Weighting/inversion is done via Woodbury identities and iterative linear algebra, making the method computationally feasible for ~10^6 sources.

2) Bias control vs ‘empirical N’ (addresses critique i–ii): By restricting correlated noise to a low-dimensional nuisance subspace with priors and by marginalizing analytically, we prevent an unconstrained empirical covariance from absorbing the SGWB signal. This is a standard, reviewer-aligned strategy: systematics are treated as parameterized modes rather than as free spatial covariance estimated from the same data.

3) TT treatment under masking and anisotropic noise (addresses critique iii): TT is enforced through a forward covariance model plus explicit window/mode-coupling, not by a hard map-level nulling. The estimator’s transfer function and leakage are measured in simulations and reported, ensuring that any signal attenuation from masking is quantified and corrected (or folded into uncertainties).

4) Statistical rigor and calibrated detection claims (addresses critique iv): The proposal now uses the exact Gaussian likelihood (including log-determinants) or a rigorously derived optimal quadratic estimator with Fisher normalization. Detection significance is calibrated against the null via end-to-end simulations containing the same nuisance priors and scan-law templates, enabling controlled false-alarm rates.

5) EOS claims made realistic (addresses critique v): Because Gaia’s response is effectively broadband and ultra-low-frequency with limited spectral resolution, the revised scope treats the neutron-star/EOS component primarily as a constrained sub-dominant contribution (η_NS) and provides an explicit identifiability/Fisher analysis. The deliverable becomes an EOS-consistent bound/consistency check rather than an over-strong claim of EOS inference unless the identifiability study demonstrates otherwise.

Critique: The methodological direction is strong and, in principle, aligned with how one should treat Gaia’s dominant low-ℓ systematics (explicit low-dimensional modes + analytic marginalization) while avoiding ad-hoc “empirical N” that can absorb SGWB correlations. However, several key elements remain under-specified at the level needed to justify the claimed optimality and bias control: (i) identifiability between TT signal covariance and the chosen nuisance subspace is asserted but not demonstrated—low-ℓ TT correlations can be partially degenerate with low-order VSH/scan templates, and the proposal lacks a concrete orthogonality/degeneracy metric and a mode-selection protocol tied to false-alarm control; (ii) the forward TT response is described at the level of pseudo-Cℓ coupling, but the actual catalog-level operator from a stochastic metric perturbation to mission-window-averaged proper motions (including time-domain response W(f), source sampling, and the E/B structure actually observable with Gaia) is not spelled out with enough mathematical specificity to assess correctness and implementability; (iii) the likelihood is labeled “exact Gaussian,” yet the computational plan for ln det and C^{-1} with ~10^6 sources is still aspirational—stochastic log-det plus signal-dependent terms can be the dominant numerical risk, and the proposal does not commit to a tractable approximation regime (e.g., bandpower parameterization, low-ℓ truncation, or explicitly low-rank signal model) with controlled error; (iv) the needlet layer adds complexity but the proposal does not prove it preserves optimality relative to a direct harmonic-space quadratic estimator given anisotropic noise and masking; without a clear argument, needlets risk becoming an aesthetic choice rather than a rigorously motivated compression. Hypothesis: Refined Hypothesis (Quantified Decision Boundary): A measurable subset of long-lived, fading soft X-ray plateaus currently classified as jetted tidal disruption events occupy a statistically identifiable region of spectral–timing response space that is consistent with neutron-star surface/boundary-layer reprocessing and inconsistent—at a calibrated false-positive rate—with any physically realistic jet + disk/wind/cocoon reprocessing model. This separation is not claimed to be absolute, but probabilistic: it emerges only when (i) causal, positive, energy-resolved transfer functions are inferred under a multi-driver variability model that allows spectral pivoting, and (ii) the inferred lag–frequency–energy structure falls within a detectability-limited window corresponding to shallow ocean / outer-envelope thermal diffusion (column depths y ≲ 10^9–10^11 g cm⁻²) plus light-crossing delays of a ~10–30 km surface. The mechanism that enables discrimination is the *joint constraint* imposed by (a) a compact reprocessing scale anchored to a hard surface, (b) diffusion-kernel shapes restricted by dense-matter thermal transport (heat capacity and conductivity), and (c) their smooth, flux-dependent evolution during the plateau decay. Extended jet, sheath, or wind reprocessors can reproduce monotonic lags in isolation, but cannot simultaneously reproduce the observed high-frequency roll-off, the energy-coupled diffusion-kernel evolution, and the calibrated Bayes-factor thresholds once realistic NICER count statistics and competing variability components are included. Thus, the outcome is a quantified classification probability (NS-like vs jet-like), not a binary claim, with explicit false-positive/false-negative rates.
Plan:
1. End-to-end identifiability and calibration study (mandatory foundation):
   - Construct a simulation library of NICER event lists (photon-level, Poisson) spanning observed EP240408a-like count rates, backgrounds, and cadences.
   - NS model family: surface + magnetosphere + outer-ocean diffusion kernels with radii R = 10–14 km; light-crossing delays τ_lc = 30–100 μs; diffusion timescale distributions τ_diff(y,D) spanning 0.1–50 s, parameterized by column depth y = 10^8–10^11 g cm⁻² and thermal diffusivity D(ρ,Ye,T) drawn from nuclear-physics transport ranges.
   - Jet null family (expanded per critique): relativistic jet internal dissipation + curvature delays; scattering photosphere; disk wind / cocoon reverberation with characteristic scales 10^2–10^6 km; include compact effective lags via stratified emission zones and electron-scattering delays. Allow combinations so the null is not artificially weak.
   - For each realization, infer transfer functions using the full pipeline and compute Bayes factors and posterior overlaps. Produce ROC curves (false-positive/false-negative rates) as functions of count rate, variability rms, and observation length. This defines the *decision boundary*.

2. Variability architecture (addressing driver assumptions):
   - Replace the single latent driver with a factor-analysis state-space model: s_k(t), k = 1…K (K = 1–3), representing broadband accretion noise, magnetospheric bursts, or spectral-pivot components.
   - Each energy band E has mixing weights w_{E,k}; transfer functions h_{E,k}(t) are inferred per factor.
   - Model selection (WAIC/Bayes evidence) determines whether K=1 is sufficient; if not, marginalize over K>1 rather than forcing a shared driver. This prevents spurious lag attribution from spectral pivoting.

3. Detectability forecast and physical timescale mapping:
   - Explicitly map diffusion parameters to observable lag amplitudes in the NICER-accessible Fourier range (≈10⁻³–10 Hz for multi-day plateaus).
   - Show that shallow ocean / envelope diffusion (τ_diff ≈ 0.3–30 s) produces measurable hard lags (≳5–50 ms) at frequencies where coherence remains high for EP240408a-like count rates, whereas deeper crustal diffusion (hours–days) is not claimed to be measurable and is excluded from inference.
   - Prior truncation is therefore physically motivated, avoiding prior-dominated EOS claims.

4. Inference pipeline (refined):
   - Photon-level likelihood with NICER response folding; causal, positive transfer functions represented via spline or log-normal bases with enforced finite support.
   - Joint inference across energies and epochs with smooth evolution hyperpriors tied to flux decay.
   - Decision metrics: Bayes factors relative to the calibrated jet null; posterior probability of compact-scale (≤30 km) reprocessor; consistency of energy-scaling with opacity-driven diffusion.

5. Multi-instrument role clarity:
   - Swift/XRT used only for flux/spectral evolution and long-timescale variability consistency, not short-timescale lag validation. NICER provides all decisive timing information.

6. Application to data:
   - Apply only within the calibrated regime identified in Step 1. Events outside this regime are reported as ‘uninformative’, preventing over-claiming.
Feasibility: This revision directly addresses reviewer concerns by replacing claims of decisiveness with a calibrated, simulation-backed decision boundary. The variability model explicitly allows multiple drivers and spectral pivoting, preventing bias from over-simplified assumptions. The nuclear-physics linkage is narrowed to shallow ocean / envelope diffusion regimes that produce lags detectable in the NICER Fourier window, avoiding overreach into unmeasurable crustal depths. Finally, the jet comparator is expanded to include disk winds, cocoons, and scattering photospheres, ensuring Bayes factors reflect genuine physical discrimination rather than model incompleteness. The EP240408a observational asset sits squarely in the regime (high soft-X-ray counts, multi-day plateau) where this calibrated approach is feasible, making the proposal technically credible, falsifiable, and appropriately scoped.
Critique: The proposal is technically sophisticated and, relative to typical lag/reverberation work, unusually careful about identifiability (photon-level simulations, explicit ROC/false-positive calibration, and a strengthened jet/disk/wind/cocoon null). This earns high marks for engineering and rationale. The main score deductions are (i) incomplete physical closure between the inferred “diffusion kernel” and a forward radiative-transfer model that predicts the full energy-dependent response (spectrum + timing) under realistic NS atmosphere/boundary-layer conditions; as written, the kernel constraints may still be partially phenomenological and risk absorbing unmodeled spectral evolution. (ii) The null family, while expanded, is not yet specified at the same level of microphysical constraint as the NS diffusion priors (e.g., electron-scattering/wind radiative diffusion with stratification can also yield smooth, flux-dependent kernel evolution); without a clearly enumerated, physically bounded jet/wind parameterization, Bayes factors may still reflect “prior sharpness” asymmetry rather than genuine separability. (iii) The detectability mapping cites lag amplitudes and coherence expectations but does not provide a concrete observing/program plan (segment lengths, gaps, stationarity tests over a multi-day decay, sensitivity to red-noise leakage/windowing), which is critical given NICER’s orbit gaps and background systematics; these can bias lag–frequency inference and transfer-function recovery if not explicitly built into the simulation/inference loop.

Hypothesis: SN 1054 was an electron-capture supernova (ECSN) whose exceptionally low ejected 56Ni mass and late-time luminosity constraints are consistent with a low-energy, low-entropy explosion that yields (i) weak radioactive heating and (ii) limited, quantifiable radial mixing of iron-group material. Because the SN 1054 dataset cannot uniquely identify a full 3D 56Ni field, we restrict the inverse problem to a demonstrably identifiable set of “radioactivity observables”: total M(56Ni), a single radial mixing-depth parameter for the IGE-rich component, and only the lowest-order anisotropy moment(s) that the data can support (dipole at most). In parallel, we decouple compact-object recoil from 56Ni geometry by explicitly parameterizing the *total* ejecta mass–velocity anisotropy (low-order momentum multipoles), fitting it jointly with the radioactive observables. The mechanistic link is then tested—not assumed—by calibrating the correlation between 56Ni anisotropy and total momentum anisotropy using suites of published multi-D ECSN simulations. We further tighten the multi-messenger link by pivoting the downstream population prediction from BH–BH to NS–NS/NS–BH systems, for which ECSN physics directly sets NS natal kicks and thus survival probabilities and gravitational-wave delay times. This yields a falsifiable prediction: an ECSN-conditioned kick kernel produces a measurable excess of long-delay NS–NS/NS–BH mergers (relative to iron-core CCSN) while simultaneously predicting low 56Ni yields and weak gamma-ray trapping consistent with SN 1054/Crab constraints—surviving marginalization over binary-evolution uncertainties via an explicit ablation study.
Plan:
Step 0 — Scope control and parameter reduction (implements mandatory directive)
0.1 Define the *identifiable* latent parameter set θ as:
  • Radioactivity block (R): M_Ni (total 56Ni mass), v_mix (a single radial mixing-depth parameter for IGE-rich material in homologous expansion), and optionally one anisotropy coefficient a1_Ni (56Ni dipole amplitude) if supported.
  • Momentum block (P): a low-order parameterization of the *total* ejecta momentum anisotropy independent of Ni: p1 (dimensionless dipole of mass-weighted velocity), and its direction n_k (2 angles). Optionally include p2 (quadrupole) only if identifiability tests justify it.
  • Global energetics: M_ej, E_k constrained by Crab filament kinematics; M_rem for recoil closure.
0.2 Explicitly *do not* attempt full 3D X_Ni(v,θ,ϕ) inference. Use a minimal basis whose coefficients map one-to-one onto identifiable observables.

Step 1 — Data likelihood construction using actual SN 1054/Crab constraints
1.1 Historical light-curve likelihood: encode plateau duration constraints and late-time visibility as censored/interval data. Construct L_hist(θ) using:
  • plateau duration window (e.g., 60–100 d consistent with ECSN models),
  • late-time magnitude limits/detections translated into bolometric bounds with nuisance parameters for extinction and bandpass corrections.
1.2 Crab energetics likelihood: L_Crab(θ) from filament proper motions + spectroscopy:
  • priors/likelihood for M_ej and E_k,
  • constraints on homologous expansion age consistency.
1.3 Non-radioactive power separation: include a pulsar spin-down luminosity model L_psr(t; φ_psr) with priors from Crab pulsar present-day P, \dot P and braking index, propagating uncertainty into late-time luminosity bounds rather than assuming negligible/known contribution.
1.4 Inner-heating constraints: incorporate 44Ti non-detection/upper limits and nebular ionization constraints into L_heat(θ) to bound late-time internal energy injection that could masquerade as gamma deposition.
1.5 Geometry/asymmetry constraints: include low-order morphological constraints (e.g., dominant asymmetry axis from line-of-sight velocity maps) as weak priors on the dipole direction n_k, without overinterpreting small-scale structure.

Step 2 — Forward model architecture (transport + minimal composition/mixing)
2.1 Homologous ejecta model:
  • Spherically averaged density profile ρ0(v) chosen from a compact family (e.g., broken power-law with fixed outer slope, free break velocity tied to E_k and M_ej).
  • Radioactivity distribution: an IGE-rich component with radial support controlled by v_mix. Implement as X_Ni(v) ∝ exp[−(v/v_mix)^α] truncated at v_max, normalized to M_Ni.
  • Optional Ni dipole: X_Ni(v,Ω)=X_Ni(v)[1 + a1_Ni Y10(Ω·n_Ni)], with |a1_Ni| constrained to keep X_Ni≥0.
2.2 Gamma-ray deposition model:
  • Monte-Carlo gamma transport for 56Ni→56Co→56Fe including Compton scattering + photoabsorption in expanding ejecta.
  • Output deposition fraction f_dep(t; θ) and emergent gamma luminosity. Bolometric model: L_bol(t)=f_dep L_decay(M_Ni)+L_psr(t; φ_psr) with nuisance thermalization efficiency for pulsar power.
2.3 Nuclear-physics feasibility (soft, not dominating): apply broad, simulation-informed priors on M_Ni and v_mix consistent with ECSN freeze-out (low-entropy, neutron-rich) but explicitly quantify prior sensitivity; do not impose high-dimensional NSE constraints that can dominate sparse data.

Step 3 — Explicit recoil model decoupled from Ni (addresses key critique)
3.1 Total momentum anisotropy parameterization:
  • Define the ejecta momentum dipole P1 = p1 (2E_k M_ej)^{1/2} in direction n_k.
  • Enforce recoil via momentum conservation: V_k = −P1 / M_rem, optionally plus a bounded neutrino-anisotropy term V_ν with a conservative prior range informed by CCSN theory.
3.2 Joint inference: infer (R,P,global,φ_psr) simultaneously from the combined likelihood L = L_hist × L_Crab × L_heat × L_geom.
3.3 Simulation calibration of Ni–momentum correlation:
  • Assemble a calibration dataset from published multi-D ECSN simulations (and, if needed, a small number of iron-core low-energy models) extracting: (a) 56Ni dipole moment a1_Ni, (b) total momentum dipole p1, (c) ejecta energy and mass.
  • Fit a hierarchical relation p1 ~ Normal(β0 + β1 a1_Ni + β2 v_mix + …, σ_corr) with wide priors, allowing weak/no correlation.
  • Use this only to *interpret* inferred a1_Ni relative to p1, not to force p1 from Ni.

Step 4 — Formal identifiability demonstration using the *actual* SN 1054/Crab likelihood
4.1 Fisher-information / local identifiability:
  • Compute the Fisher matrix (or expected information) for θ at the posterior mode using numerical derivatives of summary observables (late-time luminosity bounds, deposition fraction at key epochs, energetics constraints).
  • Report which parameter combinations are constrained (eigenvalue spectrum), demonstrating that only {M_Ni, v_mix, p1 (and possibly a1_Ni)} are identifiable.
4.2 SBI-based identifiability stress test with real-data summaries:
  • Use simulation-based inference (e.g., neural posterior estimation) over θ but with the *same* censored/interval likelihood structure as SN 1054 historical constraints.
  • Perform posterior shrinkage tests: show posterior contraction relative to priors for identifiable parameters; demonstrate non-contraction for non-identifiable ones and remove them from the model.
4.3 Prior-dominance quantification:
  • Re-run inference under at least two materially different priors for v_mix and p1 (broad vs simulation-informed) and report sensitivity; require qualitative conclusions (e.g., long-delay enhancement in NS binaries) to be robust.

Step 5 — Population synthesis target change: ECSN → NS–NS / NS–BH delay-time prediction (mandatory directive option i)
5.1 Post-SN binary mapping:
  • Use impulsive mass loss + vector kick V_k with isotropic n_k (or weakly informed by Crab axis) to compute survival probability and post-SN (a,e).
  • Compute GW inspiral delay times via Peters equations.
5.2 Mixture model of supernova channels:
  • Build a two-channel kernel: ECSN-conditioned kick distribution from this work + an iron-core CCSN kick baseline from literature.
  • Convolve with cosmic star-formation and metallicity evolution to obtain merger-rate vs redshift for NS–NS and NS–BH.
5.3 Controlled ablation study for falsifiability:
  • Vary common-envelope efficiency, natal spin assumptions, and metallicity-dependent winds across standard ranges.
  • Demonstrate which observables remain discriminating: (i) fraction of long-delay mergers, (ii) local merger rate normalization given calibration, (iii) eccentricity at formation (where relevant), and (iv) mass distribution shifts from ECSN-formed NS masses.
5.4 Comparison to GW constraints:
  • Use LVK population posteriors for NS–NS/NS–BH (rates, masses, spins where available) to compute hierarchical likelihoods for mixture fractions and validate whether an ECSN component is supported or constrained.

Step 6 — Validation deliverables and falsification
6.1 Crab/SN1054 self-consistency checks:
  • Ensure inferred M_Ni and v_mix predict late-time heating consistent with 44Ti limits and nebular ionization.
  • Ensure (M_ej, E_k) match filament kinematics.
6.2 External cross-checks on modern ECSN candidates:
  • Apply the reduced-parameter inversion (M_Ni, v_mix) to a small set of ECSN-like or low-luminosity II-P events with late-time photometry to validate the transport model and inferred mixing depths.
6.3 Simulation agreement:
  • Verify inferred p1 implies kick magnitudes consistent with the low-kick expectation for ECSNe (if supported) while allowing the data to reject that (via broad priors) if required.

Milestones (quantitative)
M1: Likelihood and forward-model code complete; reproduce published ECSN light curves with MC transport.
M2: Identifiability report: Fisher eigen-spectrum + SBI posterior contraction using actual SN1054/Crab likelihood.
M3: Joint posterior for {M_Ni, v_mix, p1} with prior sensitivity quantified.
M4: NS–NS/NS–BH delay-time kernels and ablation study; hierarchical comparison to LVK population constraints.
M5: Public release of minimal forward model + likelihood + posterior samples for reproducibility.
Feasibility:
1) Identifiability is enforced by design, not assumed. The inverse problem is reduced to a small parameter set whose imprint on observables is direct: M(56Ni) sets the decay power scale; v_mix controls the gamma-ray optical depth evolution (via column density seen by decay sites); and p1 sets the recoil via momentum conservation. We will formally demonstrate which parameters are constrained using (i) Fisher-information eigen-analysis and (ii) SBI posterior contraction under the actual censored historical-light-curve likelihood, addressing the underdetermination critique.

2) The kick inference is no longer logically tied to 56Ni as a proxy. The model fits an explicit, low-order *total* mass–velocity anisotropy parameter (p1, direction), and only then evaluates whether 56Ni anisotropy correlates with momentum anisotropy using multi-D ECSN simulations. This removes the unjustified assumption that Ni-bearing plumes dominate linear momentum while still allowing the hypothesis to be tested quantitatively.

3) The multi-messenger extension is made physically coherent by targeting NS–NS/NS–BH populations, where ECSN outcomes (NS formation, low explosion energy, potentially low kicks) directly control binary survival and delay times. This avoids the weak transfer argument to BH–BH. Falsifiability is protected via a controlled ablation study over binary-evolution uncertainties, isolating which GW observables (especially the long-delay fraction) remain diagnostic after marginalization.

4) Empirical anchoring is strengthened by leveraging Asset 2’s first-principles ECSN light-curve expectations (shock breakout/plateau/tail behavior and low 56Ni yields) and by aligning the SN1054 interpretation with Crab energetics and pulsar spin-down constraints. The forward model uses explicit gamma-ray transport (not an unconstrained emulator), but only to propagate the reduced set of physically meaningful parameters into observable bounds.

5) Deliverables are reproducible and discriminating. The proposal outputs (a) a minimal posterior over {M_Ni, v_mix, p1} for SN 1054, (b) a calibrated (or explicitly weak) Ni–momentum correlation from multi-D ECSN simulations, and (c) an ECSN-conditioned kick kernel for NS–NS/NS–BH delay-time predictions with uncertainty and ablation quantified—each component falsifiable against Crab constraints, modern ECSN-like events, and GW population statistics.
Critique: This is an unusually rigorous and self-aware proposal that directly addresses common inferential pathologies in historical supernova reconstruction. The strongest elements are (i) enforced identifiability via parameter reduction and Fisher/SBI diagnostics, (ii) explicit decoupling of radioactive geometry from recoil physics, and (iii) a physically coherent shift of the population-synthesis target to NS–NS/NS–BH systems where ECSN assumptions genuinely matter. The engineering plan is detailed and technically credible, though ambitious: Monte Carlo gamma-ray transport, hierarchical calibration from multi-D simulations, and full GW population comparisons collectively pose a nontrivial execution risk. Logical consistency is high, but not perfect: the link between a single radial mixing parameter v_mix and the diversity of plausible ECSN plume morphologies may still be overly compressed, potentially biasing deposition fractions even if formally identifiable. Evidence grounding is strong with respect to SN 1054, ECSN theory, and GW populations, but the provided 'target concept chain' explicitly references black hole mergers, which the proposal intentionally pivots away from—this is scientifically justified yet creates a partial mismatch with the stated chain. The rationale quality is high: the proposal does not merely apply existing tools but restructures the inverse problem to make falsifiability and uncertainty dominance explicit.

Hypothesis: Impulsive magnetospheric energy release events in the Galactic Center (either intrinsic to Sagittarius A*’s magnetized funnel or driven by nearby compact objects such as SGR J1745-2900) generate a force-free electrodynamic (FFE) fast-mode pulse that steepens into a magnetosonic shock and deposits a predictable fraction of its Poynting flux into surrounding molecular clouds, producing a coupled UV-flash + delayed Chandra X-ray fluorescence/light-echo signature. Methodological adaptation: we will modify standard time-dependent FFE solvers by embedding a physically constrained, reduced microphysics closure (FFE→radiation+cloud transfer) that converts the shock’s electromagnetic dissipation into UV emissivity and K-shell fluorescence, while enforcing invariants (E·B=0, B^2−E^2>0, charge conservation) via constrained transport and variational projection; this guarantees that inferred injection histories and the resulting electromagnetic counterpart templates remain consistent with force-free dynamics and with radiative transfer through clumpy molecular clouds. Mechanism: in FFE, an impulsive twist/reconnection event launches a fast magnetosonic disturbance with dominantly transverse fields; geometric focusing near the central engine and non-linear steepening create current sheets where dissipation occurs. The dissipated Poynting flux accelerates electrons that (i) produce prompt UV via synchrotron/curvature components and (ii) irradiate nearby molecular material; in dense clouds, photoionization yields UV reprocessing and Fe Kα fluorescence, producing an X-ray echo observable with Chandra. Because FFE fixes the field topology and energy flux transport, the UV-to-X-ray (echo) energy partition and timing are not free parameters but are constrained by field invariants, cloud column density, and light-travel geometry—enabling a physically grounded electromagnetic counterpart model for Galactic-center transients.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Compile Chandra archival event lists and imaging for Sgr A* region covering known flare epochs and molecular-cloud Fe Kα echo monitoring; extract time-resolved spectra/light curves for candidate reflection nebulae (e.g., Sgr B2-like substructures) and for the central point source region with careful pileup and background treatment.
1.2 Assemble molecular cloud 3D/kinematic priors from existing CO/CS line surveys (positions, velocity components, approximate distances) to build a probabilistic light-travel-time kernel for each cloud clump.
1.3 Define a small set of physically motivated injection scenarios: (A) Sgr A* funnel twist/reconnection; (B) magnetar-driven pulse; (C) hybrid. For each, specify initial magnetic topology and characteristic scales consistent with measured Galactic-center field constraints.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Implement a time-dependent, general-relativistic-appropriate FFE module in a simplified Kerr background (or pseudo-Newtonian approximation for targeted radii), using constrained-transport evolution for B and a variational projection step each timestep to enforce E·B=0 and B^2−E^2>0; include a positivity-preserving limiter that prevents superluminal drift in under-resolved current sheets.
2.2 Methodological adaptation (key): couple the FFE solver to a reduced dissipation+emission closure at current sheets: introduce an invariant-based dissipation functional Q = α * max(0, J·E) constrained so that global energy conservation holds (Poynting flux loss equals radiated+particle energy gain), and map Q into a two-channel emissivity model—prompt UV (synchrotron/curvature-like with parameters tied to local B and dissipation scale) plus an ionizing/X-ray photon field.
2.3 Propagate the ionizing photon field through a clumpy molecular-cloud transfer model: compute photoabsorption, UV reprocessing, and Fe Kα fluorescence yields using column-density dependent cross sections; convolve with the 3D light-travel-time kernel to generate predicted delayed Chandra-band light echoes.
2.4 Inference: perform Bayesian fitting of injection timescales, total injected electromagnetic energy, and topology parameters using both (i) prompt UV constraints (from available UV surveys/upper limits; if absent, treat as censored data) and (ii) Chandra time-resolved Fe Kα and continuum echoes. Priors enforce causality/energy limits and FFE invariants, preventing unphysical solutions that standard black-box flare templates would allow.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Internal consistency checks: verify divergence-free B, invariant satisfaction statistics, and energy budgets (injected vs radiated+echoed) across resolutions; show convergence of echo predictions with mesh refinement near current sheets.
3.2 External validation against alternative models: compare to purely phenomenological flare+reflection models and to MHD-only models without invariant projection; quantify improvement via Bayes factors and predictive performance on held-out echo epochs.
3.3 Nuclear/high-energy constraints: use the inferred ionizing spectrum to predict accompanying neutrino/MeV–GeV signatures and pair-production opacity constraints; check consistency with known limits and with plausible compact-object energetics.
3.4 Deliverables: a library of physically constrained electromagnetic counterpart templates (prompt UV + delayed Chandra echo) for Galactic-center magnetospheric transients, and posterior constraints on event energetics and geometry relevant to compact-object environments near Sgr A*.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: FFE has a strong track record for magnetospheres where plasma inertia is negligible, and prior merger-magnetosphere studies show fast-mode pulses steepen into shocks/current sheets that dissipate electromagnetic energy (Asset 1). Separately, UV/X-ray early counterparts are sensitive diagnostics of shock cooling and energy deposition (Asset 2). Chandra observations demonstrate that energetic fronts in the Galactic Center plausibly irradiate molecular clouds and produce detectable echoes/fluorescence (Asset 3).
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Standard echo modeling treats the irradiating flare spectrum as a free function, while standard FFE simulations stop at field evolution without predicting observables in molecular material. The proposed adaptation bridges these by enforcing force-free invariants during field evolution (respecting causality and electromagnetic constraints) and by attaching a minimal, energy-conserving dissipation-to-radiation closure plus cloud transfer. This directly targets the limiting gap: lack of physically constrained mapping from compact-object electromagnetic dynamics to UV/X-ray observables in the Galactic-center environment.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with unconstrained light-curve fitting, the invariant-enforcing FFE+transfer model reduces degeneracy between flare energetics, beaming, and cloud geometry by tying observables to field topology and Poynting flux transport. Compared with MHD-only approaches, it avoids poorly constrained plasma loading in the low-inertia regime and provides robust, symmetry- and conservation-respecting predictions. The result is tighter, physically interpretable constraints on the energy release mechanism near Sagittarius A* and on how that energy couples into molecular clouds, leveraging Chandra’s unique angular resolution and timing baseline.
Critique: This is a technically ambitious and largely well-structured proposal that demonstrates strong command of force-free electrodynamics, Galactic-center astrophysics, and X-ray reflection phenomenology. The core logical chain—impulsive magnetospheric energy release producing an FFE fast-mode pulse that dissipates and drives UV + Fe Kα echoes—is internally consistent and grounded in known physics. The invariant-enforcing FFE framework is a genuine strength and addresses a real degeneracy problem in echo modeling. However, there are two substantive weaknesses that limit the top score. First, the dissipation/emission closure remains under-justified at the microphysical level: while J·E-based dissipation is plausible, the mapping from electromagnetic dissipation to specific UV and ionizing spectra is still phenomenological and may not be uniquely constrained by FFE invariants alone. Second, the feasibility risk is nontrivial: GR-FFE with current-sheet-localized dissipation, coupled to radiative transfer and Bayesian inference, is computationally heavy, and the proposal underestimates the challenge of achieving numerical convergence and parameter identifiability with existing Chandra data quality. These issues do not invalidate the concept, but they weaken claims of predictiveness and robustness.

Hypothesis:
Nearly spherical accretion onto a rapidly spinning, moderately magnetized neutron star (A0538-66–like; B ~ 10^10–10^12 G at the footprint depending on multipolarity) generically admits a *magnetically anisotropic, 2D-stable* microphysical bifurcation in the near-surface settling/impact region: as the local mass flux per unit area \(\dot m(\theta,t)\) rises, the Coulomb stopping column \(y_s\) of infalling ions (computed with B-modified Coulomb drag and pitch-angle diffusion) crosses the *direction-dependent* radiative diffusion column \(y_{\rm diff,\parallel/\perp}\) of the heated electrons/radiation field. When \(y_s \approx y_{\rm diff}\), feedback among (i) ion energy deposition profile, (ii) Compton heating/cooling, and (iii) pair-assisted opacity produces a *sharp* transition from a dense, efficiently cooled, charge-rich boundary layer to an optically thinner, Compton-heated, pair-regulated layer in which the emergent low-entropy charge supply to open field lines drops rapidly.

The refined mechanism overcomes the reviewer-identified risks by explicitly demonstrating (1) that the threshold remains sharp once (a) field-guided inflow and lateral radiative leakage are included in axisymmetry, and (b) B-dependent scattering/transport and ion stopping are treated self-consistently; and (2) that the radio burst energetics and observability are closed by a quantitative mapping from gap power and pair multiplicity to escaping radio energy and spectrum under induced-scattering and free-free constraints in the inner wind.

In this picture, FRB-like bursts are produced by *charge-starvation episodes* in the polar-cap/current-closure circuit. When the surface column enters the hot/pair-regulated state, the number flux of charges with sufficiently low enthalpy to supply \(J_{\rm req}\) collapses on a microphysical timescale comparable to (or shorter than) the magnetospheric gap growth time. The magnetosphere responds by developing \(E_\parallel\), initiating a pair cascade. A calculable fraction \(\epsilon_{\rm rad}\) of the gap power is converted into coherent radio emission via curvature-driven bunching/maser (mode-dependent) in a pair-loaded plasma, with emission frequency set by the local plasma/curvature scales and the spectrum/escape set by induced Compton/Raman and wind free-free absorption. The per-system burst efficiency is anchored directly to A0538-66 observables via a pre-registered compactness/luminosity threshold and a predicted spectral pivot/hardness behavior. Convolving this per-system burst rate with the redshift-dependent formation rate of A0538-66 analog Be/XRBs yields an FRB source formation rate vs redshift; the proposal also explicitly contrasts why an analogous mechanism is suppressed or altered in black-hole accretors (no surface stopping layer; no anchored current-closure gap at a conducting surface), making the NS surface an essential ingredient.

Critique: This is an unusually detailed and technically mature proposal that squarely addresses prior reviewer concerns rather than deflecting them. The strongest aspect is the insistence on *measured sharpness* of the y_s ≈ y_diff transition in 2D with B-modified transport, which converts a speculative bifurcation into a falsifiable numerical result. The pre-registration of a compactness threshold and spectral pivot in A0538-66 is exemplary and rare in high-energy theory proposals. Logical consistency is high: the surface stopping layer → charge starvation → gap growth → coherent radio emission chain is physically motivated and explicitly closed with energy and opacity constraints. Deductions arise mainly from feasibility risk rather than conceptual flaws: the proposed 2D solver simultaneously handling kinetic ion stopping, anisotropic FLD+Kompaneets transport, and pair balance at millisecond cadence is extremely demanding and may exceed realistic development time. Additionally, the coherent radio emission step still relies on a phenomenological efficiency parameter (ε_coh) and a pre-selected emission channel; while constrained, this remains the least first-principles component. Evidence grounding is strong, though the Be-wind propagation and induced-scattering treatment is necessarily semi-analytic and could become a dominant uncertainty if densities are higher than assumed.

Hypothesis: In accreting millisecond X-ray pulsars (AMXPs), the dominant bias in inferred pulse frequency and its derivative arises from flux-driven, energy-dependent photon travel-time redistribution through a dynamically varying, Comptonizing accretion shock/column and boundary layer—not from geometric hot-spot wandering. Mechanism: as accretion rate (traced by X-ray flux/luminosity) changes, the optical depth and temperature of the scattering region above the magnetic polar cap/boundary layer change, producing energy-dependent time lags and pulse-shape distortions that shift the Fourier phase of the fundamental/harmonics without requiring any physical change in stellar spin. Methodological adaptation: replace phase–flux detrending and explicit spot-geometry motion models with a causality-preserving, radiative-transfer-informed timing estimator that models the observed pulse train as the intrinsic (spin-locked) emission convolved with a flux-dependent, energy-dependent impulse response function (IRF) derived from constrained Comptonization physics (Kompaneets limit + light-travel time constraints) and magnetospheric energy budget bounds. This ‘deconvolution timing’ separates intrinsic rotational phase evolution from propagation-induced phase shifts, enabling a physically consistent torque–luminosity test and, via compactness-sensitive lag bounds, joint constraints on neutron-star M/R and the nuclear equation of state (EoS) without assuming moving hot spots.

Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.

Target systems: assemble a sample spanning luminosity states and pulse frequencies, including at least one ultracompact low-\dot{M} AMXP (e.g., IGR J17494-3030-like; Asset 2) and multiple outbursting AMXPs with known phase–flux correlations (Asset 3). 3. Flux/luminosity calibration: compute absorbed/unabsorbed fluxes and bolometric corrections with spectral fits; propagate distance priors to luminosity; quantify systematic uncertainties (instrument cross-cal, background).

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
1. Generative pulse-transfer model (core adaptation): model the observed photon time series in each energy band E as
   x_E(t) = [s(t; \nu, \dot{\nu}, orbit) * h_E(t; \Theta(t))] + b_E(t),
   where s(t) is the intrinsic spin-locked pulse train (including harmonics), and h_E is an energy-dependent impulse response function (IRF) representing scattering/propagation in the accretion shock/column/boundary layer; \Theta(t) are physical state parameters tied to accretion rate.
2. Physics-constrained IRF family:
   - Use a minimum-parameter IRF whose moments are physically interpretable and bounded: mean delay \langle\tau_E\rangle, variance \sigma^2_{\tau,E}, and a causal tail index. Enforce strict causality: h_E(\tau<0)=0, \int h_E d\tau = 1.
   - Link \langle\tau_E\rangle and \sigma_{\tau,E} to Comptonization and size constraints: optical depth \tau_T(t), electron temperature kT_e(t), and characteristic size \ell(t) with \ell \le f\,R (f<~a few), so \langle\tau\rangle \sim (N_{sc}/c)\lambda and N_{sc} consistent with Kompaneets y-parameter (y \approx 4kT_e/m_ec^2\,\max(\tau_T,\tau_T^2)). This ties timing lags directly to spectral hardness and flux.
   - Enforce energy and angular-momentum budgets: luminosity sets maximum heating power available to the scattering region; require that inferred Compton y and coronal heating fraction do not exceed L_X.
3. Frequency-domain deconvolution timing estimator:
   - Work in Fourier domain for each segment. The complex Fourier coefficient at harmonic n and energy E satisfies X_{n,E} = S_n \cdot H_{n,E}(\Theta) + noise. Here H_{n,E} is the Fourier transform of h_E.
   - Jointly fit across energies and harmonics to infer (i) the intrinsic rotational phase evolution (\nu, \dot{\nu}), and (ii) the IRF parameters \Theta(t) that vary with flux.
   - Key identifiability lever: intrinsic spin shifts produce energy-independent phase drifts at fixed harmonic, while propagation IRF produces an energy-dependent phase \arg H_{n,E} and amplitude attenuation |H_{n,E}|; constrain both using the measured cross-spectral lags and pulsed fractions.
4. Nuclear/EoS constraint injection without geometric spot modeling:
   - Use compactness bounds through maximum allowed light-travel delay across the emitting region: \ell \le \alpha R and R(M) drawn from causal, thermodynamically stable EoS families satisfying M_max \ge 2\,M\odot. This places an upper limit on delays and IRF widths in the neutron-star frame.
   - Include GR redshift factor in mapping between local and observed timescales: \tau_obs = \tau_local (1+z), with 1+z=(1-2GM/Rc^2)^{-1/2}. This couples timing-lag bounds to M/R, enabling EoS-sensitive inference from timing+spectral data.
5. Torque–luminosity inference (secondary deliverable):
   - After removing propagation-induced phase shifts, measure intrinsic \dot{\nu}. Compare with accretion-torque prescriptions across luminosity states, testing for propeller/transition behavior using corrected \dot{\nu}(L_X).

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
1. End-to-end simulations (injection/recovery):
   - Generate synthetic AMXP data with known \nu, \dot{\nu}, binary parameters, and a flux-driven IRF that reproduces observed energy-dependent lags; add realistic counting noise and background. Verify unbiased recovery of \dot{\nu} and correct uncertainty calibration.
   - Stress tests: (i) purely intrinsic spin torque with no IRF evolution, (ii) mixed intrinsic+IRF evolution, (iii) non-stationary red noise. Confirm the estimator does not falsely attribute intrinsic \dot{\nu} to IRF changes.
2. Model comparison:
   - Compare (A) conventional TOA timing with polynomial noise, (B) phase–flux linear corrections, (C) the proposed IRF-deconvolution model. Use predictive checks on held-out segments and Bayes factors/WAIC.
3. Multi-observable consistency checks:
   - Verify that inferred IRF parameters predict the observed energy-dependent pulsed amplitude suppression and phase lags simultaneously.
   - Check that inferred kT_e and \tau_T from timing are consistent with spectral fits (e.g., Comptonization model parameters) within uncertainties.
4. Cross-context extension to high-energy sources:
   - Apply the same IRF-lag framework to distinguish pulsed emission vs external-shock dominated X-ray flux in ambiguous high-energy transients (Asset 4): a true pulsar engine predicts coherent, energy-dependent lag structure tied to Comptonization; an external shock should not show coherent harmonic-resolved IRF signatures.
5. EoS robustness:
   - Repeat inference under multiple causal EoS parameterizations; report which timing-lag constraints are EoS-driven vs instrument/systematic-driven; verify no posterior mass-radius samples violate causality or 2\,M\odot support.

Compactness enters through light-travel-time bounds and redshift, enabling EoS-sensitive inference compatible with nuclear-physics constraints.

It provides: (i) unbiased pulse frequency/\dot{\nu} estimates even under strong phase–flux correlations, (ii) a direct mechanistic link between timing lags and spectral Comptonization parameters, and (iii) an independent, causality-based route to constrain M/R and EoS through maximum allowable delays, all while being testable via injection studies and predictive validation.
Critique: This is a technically ambitious and largely coherent proposal that addresses a well-known bottleneck in AMXP timing: flux-correlated phase noise that contaminates spin and torque inference. The central hypothesis—propagation-induced, energy-dependent phase shifts dominating over geometric hot-spot motion—is physically plausible and articulated with substantially more rigor than typical phenomenological treatments. The engineering plan is detailed, with a clear generative model, Fourier-domain estimator, and validation pathway. However, some score deductions are warranted. First, identifiability between intrinsic harmonic content of s(t) and higher-moment structure of the IRF is asserted but not fully proven; in particular, degeneracies between harmonic-dependent beaming and energy-dependent IRF phase could persist in low-S/N regimes. Second, the EoS inference lever, while conceptually appealing, is weakly constraining in practice: light-travel-time bounds across a compact scattering region are likely to produce only upper limits that are subdominant to systematic uncertainties (distance, coronal geometry, spectral model degeneracy). Third, the reliance on simplified Kompaneets-limit Comptonization may break down in magnetized, bulk-flow-dominated accretion columns, potentially biasing the IRF parameter–spectral parameter mapping. These issues do not invalidate the approach but limit the strength of some claimed secondary deliverables.
